test_title: RRB Group D Official Paper (Held On: 23 Dec, 2025 Shift 3)
subject: general
question: Why are ceilings of concert halls often made curved?

options.text: To reduce the speed of sound in air
To reflect sound uniformly in all directions
To absorb sound and reduce loudness

solution:
The correct answer is __**To reflect sound uniformly in all directions**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The ceilings of **concert halls**, **conference halls**, and **cinema halls** are designed with a **curved shape** so that sound, after **reflection** from the ceiling, reaches all corners of the hall.
 
• This design ensures the **uniform distribution** of sound waves, allowing the audience to hear the performance clearly regardless of their seating position. ***Hence, statement 3 is correct.***
 
• A **curved ceiling** acts like a large **concave reflector**. When sound waves hit the curved surface, they are reflected back toward the floor in a spreading pattern, covering a larger **area** than a flat ceiling would.
 
• The curvature does not stop **reverberation**; in fact, controlled reverberation is often desirable in music halls for a richer sound. ***Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.***
 
• The **speed of sound** is a physical property of the **medium** (air) and is affected by **temperature** and **humidity**, not by the shape of the ceiling. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***
 
• While certain materials are used to **absorb sound** to prevent **echoes**, the specific purpose of the **curved shape** itself is reflection and distribution rather than absorption. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Soundboard:** In many large auditoriums, a curved **soundboard** is placed behind the speaker or the stage. The source of sound is placed at the **focus** of the board, so the reflected sound travels as a **parallel beam** toward the audience.
 
• **Reverberation:** This is the **persistence of sound** in a hall due to repeated reflections. If the **reverberation time** is too long, sound overlaps and becomes distorted. To control this, **sound-absorbent materials** like **compressed fiberboard** or **heavy draperies** are used on walls.
 
• **Multiple Reflection of Sound:** This principle is utilized in various instruments and devices. For example, in a **stethoscope**, the sound of the patient's heartbeat reaches the doctor's ears by **multiple reflections** inside the tube.
 
• **Echo:** An echo is the sound heard after reflection from a distant obstacle. To hear a distinct echo, the **time interval** between the original sound and the reflected one must be at least **0.1 seconds**. At a standard temperature of **22 degrees Celsius**, the minimum distance required for an echo is **17.2 meters**.
 
• **Acoustics:** The branch of science that deals with the production, control, transmission, reception, and effects of sound is known as **Acoustics**. Proper **acoustic engineering** is vital for the construction of **theaters** and **stadiums**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Reflection Laws:** Sound follows the same laws of **reflection** as light, where the **angle of incidence** is equal to the **angle of reflection**, and all rays lie in the same **plane**.
 
• **Intensity:** Curved surfaces help in maintaining the **intensity** of the sound over long distances by preventing the sound energy from scattering into the upper atmosphere of the building.
 
• **Shape:** While ceilings are often **parabolic** or **spherical** in curve to optimize focus, the general **cylindrical** or curved design is the most common standard for **architectural acoustics**.
</ul
